comparator.academicYear: Current programme and 2026-2027 course continuity checked 2026-10-07; latest complete official curriculum table 2025-2026
comparator.sourceNotes: The current programme and live 2026-2027 course records confirm the continuing Dutch-taught Computer Science bachelor and its programming, mathematical, systems, data and AI curriculum. The latest complete target-specific programme table supplies one coherent 180-EC pathway. Years 1 and 2 each contain 60 EC of compulsory study. The third year contains 30 EC of genuine minor/free-choice space, 15 EC for the Bachelor Thesis Project, 3 EC of AI and Ethics, 6 EC of Software Engineering and 6 EC of advanced free-choice study, instantiated by the first-listed eligible 6-EC option Applied Data Science and Explainable AI. The guide displays Machine Learning in both Years 2 and 3 because it serves transitioning cohorts; the coherent entrant pathway counts it once in Year 2 and uses the separately documented 6-EC Year-3 choice instead. The target is the standard Computer Science bachelor, not the separately normalized Data Science and Artificial Intelligence programme or a double/combined route.

alternatives.labelRationale: This curriculum retains programming, databases, algorithms, software and mathematics while shifting four courses from the closest route toward computer vision, robotics, experimental statistics and brain-and-behaviour foundations. Its centre is computational work with data and learning systems rather than software and systems alone.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Compared with the closest route, this programme replaces Networks & Operating Systems, Advanced Algorithms, rhetorical communication and general philosophy with Computer Vision, Robotics, Statistics & Experimental Methods and Introduction to Brain & Behavior. The different courses are direct consequences of its data, learning and embodied-intelligence focus, not numerical substitutions.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Introduction to Programming and Logic & Discrete Mathematics establish programming and formal foundations in semester 1. Mathematical Methods in semester 2 precedes all dependent mathematics; Introduction to Programming precedes Networks & Operating Systems, Algorithms & Data Structures, Software Development, Advanced Algorithms and later AI courses. Networks & Operating Systems is taken at its sole planned offering in semester 3. Research Methods and foundational mathematics precede advanced computational, data and AI work. Every course is available in its assigned term and every formal prerequisite is completed earlier.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest alternative owns Computer Science's programming, algorithms, software, databases, networks, operating systems and mathematical foundations. The target evidence also supports two coherent and materially different directions: data and statistical learning, and artificial intelligence linked to cognition, interaction and responsible systems. Their schedules replace substantial groups of systems/software or data-oriented courses with concept-driven alternatives, and every pair differs by at least four courses. The maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both establish structured and object-oriented programming, testing, debugging and computational problem-solving foundations.
Both cover operating-system resource management and Internet architecture and protocols through practical computational work.
Both cover relational databases, SQL, data modelling, normalization and query processing.
Both develop software through requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance and quality assurance.
Both teach algorithm design, data structures and performance analysis.
Advanced Algorithms addresses computational efficiency and algorithmic solution methods, while Leiden's component gives a dedicated formal treatment of complexity.
Both develop the structured communication and presentation of academic or technical arguments; Leiden situates this specifically in computer-science study.
UCR has one introductory programming course and a later software-development course, but no separate second compulsory programming-techniques module at Leiden's weight.
UCR does not offer a dedicated digital logic and hardware-design course.
UCR's Networks & Operating Systems discusses hardware/software interaction but does not reproduce a dedicated computer-architecture course.
UCR Software Development uses C++ and Haskell but does not reproduce Leiden's separate programming-language-concepts component.
UCR includes responsible-computing and systems perspectives but no dedicated technical cybersecurity course in the fixed portfolio.
Both establish calculus and mathematical problem-solving used in computing.
Both cover matrices, vector spaces, transformations and eigenvalues.
Advanced Calculus extends the calculus foundation to multiple dimensions and differential equations.
Both establish probability distributions, inference and probabilistic reasoning for computing.
Both provide logic and discrete structures for formal computational reasoning.
No single UCR course reproduces Leiden's dedicated theoretical Foundations of Computer Science module.
UCR has no dedicated automata-theory component.
Algorithms & Data Structures is already aligned to Leiden's algorithms module and cannot be counted twice as the separate second-year data-structures course.
UCR has no dedicated formal-languages and computability course.
UCR offers one logic-and-discrete-mathematics course rather than Leiden's two-stage logic sequence.
Both involve practical data preparation, analysis, visualization and interpretation, though Leiden's advanced elective adds explainable AI.
Both teach regression, classification, clustering and evaluation of predictive models.
Both examine fairness, responsibility, privacy and ethical questions raised by artificial intelligence.
Both cover computational search, optimisation and reasoning for artificial intelligence.
Both teach statistical modelling and experimental analysis, though Leiden frames the methods specifically for computer scientists.
Both develop research design, operationalisation, experiments, sampling and statistical inference; Leiden applies them specifically within computer science.
Both support academic orientation, study development and reflective professional formation.
UCR has no scheduled bachelor-thesis course; the standardized optional independent-research opportunity is placed against this component.
Leiden's genuine 30-EC minor or free-choice space is preserved without inventing a subject.

notes.text: Both curricula can include substantial programming, algorithms, databases, software development, operating systems, networks, mathematics, data science and artificial intelligence. Leiden additionally provides a fixed sequence in digital systems, computer architecture, automata, formal languages and computability, two-stage logic, technical security, programming-language concepts and a compulsory 15-EC thesis. UCR does not reproduce those specialist components at the same depth.

Leiden organises Computer Science as a tightly sequenced disciplinary bachelor with small-credit modules and a large third-year choice space. UCR distributes related study across 7.5-EC courses in computer science, mathematics, data science, artificial intelligence, cognition and philosophy, producing coherent liberal-arts routes rather than the same course-by-course structure.
